Empirical Research Plan: “Control Rights and Capital Structure”

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Fuzzy Regression-Discontinuity Design (RDD) complemented by an event-study Difference-in-Differences (DiD).

Why RDD?  
• When a financial covenant is violated (slack < 0), lenders obtain additional control rights almost mechanically.  
• The running variable (covenant slack = accounting ratio – covenant threshold) is continuous and (within a narrow neighborhood) plausibly not manipulated by the firm ex-ante.  
• Outcomes (leverage) observed after the test date can therefore be compared for firms just above vs. just below the cutoff.

Why fuzzy?  
• Some violations are waived, and in some near-misses lenders still renegotiate control rights. Hence covenant violation changes the probability, not certainty, of additional rights.

Why also an event-study DiD?  
• To show dynamic responses (pre-trends, anticipation) and to broaden external validity beyond a narrow bandwidth.  
• DiD is implemented by interacting a “Post-Violation” dummy with a “Ever-Violator” indicator and including firm and calendar-time fixed effects.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definitions
------------------------------------------------------------
Running variable (R): Covenant Slack = (Actual accounting ratio – Covenant threshold) / |threshold|, measured at the test date for each loan.

Cutoff: R = 0.  
• R < 0  → “Assigned to treatment” (creditors gain control rights with high probability).  
• R ≥ 0 → “Assigned to control”.

Treatment variable (D): Indicator that additional control rights are actually granted (e.g., an increase of ≥1 point in a Control-Rights Index constructed from covenant amendments). Because D jumps but not from 0→1 with certainty, the design is fuzzy.

Timing: The test date quarter (or month) when slack is assessed is event time t = 0. Outcome windows t = +1, +2, … quarters.

Control group: Firms with R just above 0 in the same test date (RDD) or firms that never violate within the sample window (DiD benchmark).

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
For the RDD:

A1. Continuity: All potential determinants of leverage evolve smoothly in R around 0.  
• Plausible: covenant thresholds are written years earlier; small infra-marginal shocks push firms across 0.

A2. No precise manipulation of R at 0.  
• Plausible: managers learn slack only after period closes, limited short-term ability to fine-tune.

A3. First-stage relevance: P(D = 1 | R < 0) – P(D = 1 | R > 0) ≠ 0.  
• Empirically testable; prior literature shows jumps of 25–40 p.p.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers across firms).  
• Reasonable at firm level.

For the DiD:

B1. Parallel trends: Absent violations, leverage of eventual violators would have evolved like that of non-violators.  
• Event-study pre-trend coefficients will be inspected.

B2. No simultaneous shocks differentially affecting treated.  
• Addressed with firm×time-varying controls and industry×year FE.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Financial distress confounds treatment (violations occur when performance deteriorates and firms may delever anyway).  
• RDD: Local comparison reduces performance differences. Covariate balance tests & inclusion of running variable polynomial.  
• IV approach: Use violation as instrument for actual control-rights change and control for contemporaneous performance.

T2. Measurement error in covenant slack.  
• Use lender-reported test dates and thresholds, winsorize extreme slack, replicate results with alternative slack definitions (e.g., raw dollar breach).

T3. Waivers / renegotiations weaken first stage (fuzzy design).  
• Estimate first stage explicitly; report Local Average Treatment Effect. Robustness: restrict to non-waived violations, or instrument by “non-waived violation”.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Load packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast FE regressions
library(rdrobust)    # RD estimation

# 1. Data loading ------------------------------------------------------------
ds  <- fread("dealscan_loans.csv")   # loan-level covenants
comp<- fread("compustat_fundq.csv")  # quarterly accounting
link<- fread("link_table.csv")       # linking table

# 2. Merge & variable construction ------------------------------------------
# Create firm-quarter panel
ds[, quarter := as.yearqtr(test_date)]
cov <- merge(ds, link, by="dealID")
cov <- merge(cov, comp, by=c("gvkey","quarter"), all.x=TRUE)

# Covenant slack
cov[, slack := (actual_ratio - threshold)/abs(threshold)]

# Violation indicator
cov[, violation := as.integer(slack < 0)]

# Change in control rights (ΔCR index) – assume variable cr_index
setorder(cov, gvkey, test_date)
cov[, cr_change := cr_index - shift(cr_index), by=gvkey]
cov[, treat := as.integer(cr_change > 0)]   # realized treatment

# Leverage outcome (book leverage)
cov[, lev := total_debt / total_assets]

# 3. Fuzzy RDD --------------------------------------------------------------
# Keep observations in ±20% slack window
rd <- cov[slack > -0.2 & slack < 0.2]

# First stage: effect of violation on treatment
fs <- rdrobust(y = rd$treat, x = rd$slack, c = 0)
print(fs)

# Second stage: effect on leverage
ss <- rdrobust(y = rd$lev, x = rd$slack, c = 0, fuzzy = rd$treat)
print(ss)

# 4. Event-study DiD --------------------------------------------------------
# Define event time relative to first violation
cov[, first_vio_qtr := min(quarter[violation==1]), by=gvkey]
cov[, rel_qtr := as.integer(quarter - first_vio_qtr)]

# Keep ±8 quarters
es <- cov[rel_qtr >= -8 & rel_qtr <= 8]

# Create event-time dummies
for(k in -8:8) es[, paste0("d",k) := as.integer(rel_qtr==k)]

# Regression with firm and calendar-quarter FE; omit d-1
fml <- as.formula(paste(
  "lev ~",
  paste(paste0("d", -8:8)[-9], collapse="+"),    # exclude d-1
  "+ control_vars | gvkey + quarter"
))
est <- feols(fml, data=es, cluster="gvkey")
etable(est)

# 5. Robustness: alternative bandwidth ±10% -------------------------------
rd2 <- cov[slack > -0.1 & slack < 0.1]
ss2 <- rdrobust(y = rd2$lev, x = rd2$slack, c = 0, fuzzy = rd2$treat)
print(ss2)
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition: When creditors gain control rights, they can restrict further borrowing and may force asset sales or equity issuance, leading to a decline in financial leverage.

Prior expectation: 4–8 percentage-point drop in book leverage (debt/TA) within one year after a violation for the marginal firm at the cutoff. Sign should be negative.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)
------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Discontinuity in treatment probability at cutoff: 1  
C2. No manipulation of running variable (McCrary density test): 0.8  
C3. Covariate balance within bandwidth: 0.8  
C4. Robust to bandwidth / polynomial choices: 0.7  
C5. Placebo cutoffs & falsification outcomes: 0.8  

(Overall average ≈ 0.82 → design appears credible but will require careful robustness work.)
